newsitem.title: USA: Dole fumes while Clinton courts voters.
newsitem.headline: Dole fumes while Clinton courts voters.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent

Ross Perot on Thursday spurned Bob Dole's request to quit the White House race, leaving the Republican to fume about public apathy while President Bill Clinton courted voters with his message of peace and prosperity.

Speaking at the National Press Club in Washington, Reform Party candidate Perot declined directly to criticise Dole, who sent his campaign manager to Dallas on Wednesday in a vain attempt to persuade the outspoken Texan to drop out and back Dole against Clinton.
"Am I in this for the long haul? Yes. Do I intend to campaign to the bitter end? Yes," Perot said in response to a question. He called the Dole appeal "weird and totally inconsequential."
In Pensacola, Florida, Dole ignored questions about the Perot overture but frustration with his stalled campaign bubbled over into an angry critique of the American public and the media.
"This is a very important election. And I know everybody gets frustrated. I even get frustrated and I'm the most optimistic man in America," the former Kansas senator said.
"I wonder sometimes what people are thinking about or if people are thinking at all if they've really watched this administration, watched what's happening in the White House," he said.
"We need to wake America up. It's 12 days away. Wake up, America! You're about to do yourselves an injustice if you vote for Bill Clinton."
Dole also targeted what he called "the liberal media," accusing it of trying to boost Clinton to a second term.
"The media will not decide the winner of this election. You'll decide who wins this election," he said.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry, in Lake Charles, Louisiana, with Clinton, called Dole's attack ill-advised.
"As a general practice, in my time in politics, I think it's best not to accuse the American people of not thinking when you are trying to earn their support and trust," he said.
Clinton campaigned in the Republican-leaning Deep South, secure in the knowledge that polls remained heavily in his favour with 12 days until the Nov. 5 election.

"Even though our friends on the other side don't like to admit it, we are better off than we were four years ago, and we are moving in the right direction," he told a rally in Birmingham, Alabama, a state solidly Republican in recent races but where Clinton is only a few points behind Dole.
Polls showed a slight tightening in the race on Thursday -- but too little, too late, to suggest a real difference.
The Reuters daily tracking poll had Clinton leading by around 9 percentage points among likely voters. Other surveys put his lead at between 12 and 16 points.
Analysts said Dole's appeal to Perot would not have helped much even if the Texan had agreed to withdraw, because his support was only in the 4-8 percent range.
But some analysts said the appeal and the public rejection it drew made Dole look weak and could harm him further.

"This admission of weakness could diminish Dole's prospects in the home stretch. It may demoralise Republican activists and potentially hurt the party all the way down the ticket," said American University analyst Mark Rozell.
Relishing a rare opportunity to bask in the spotlight, Perot launched a bitter attack on Clinton's ethics and warned that the country was headed for a financial meltdown and a Wall Street crash.

"We are heading toward a second Watergate with all this stuff going on and a constitutional crisis in 1997 and just remember you heard it here first," he said in his press club speech, complaining that the media was ignoring his message.
The White House dismissed Perot's Watergate charge. "I think that's certainly not the president's view of the future. Ross Perot has to speak for himself," McCurry said.
